title: ATLS primary survey & thoracic trauma
subject: Surgery
anchor: Primary survey ABCDE (airway with cervical-spine protection first); treat each life threat as you find it — never wait for X-ray to decompress a tension pneumothorax.
Distended neck veins + hyperresonance + absent breath sounds + shock = tension pneumothorax; flat neck veins + dullness + shock = massive haemothorax.
Distended neck veins + muffled heart sounds + hypotension (Beck triad) with equal breath sounds = cardiac tamponade.
algorithm:
Primary survey: control exsanguinating external bleeding → A (airway + C-spine restriction) → B → C → D → E
  B: absent breath sounds + shock
    Hyperresonant, trachea away, neck veins full → TENSION PTX
      → immediate needle/finger decompression (clinical diagnosis, no CXR) → chest tube
    Dull, neck veins flat → MASSIVE HAEMOTHORAX
      → large-bore chest tube (5th ICS, anterior to mid-axillary line) + blood
      → thoracotomy if ≥1500 mL immediately or >200 mL/h for 2–4 h, or ongoing transfusion need
    Sucking wound → OPEN PTX → 3-sided dressing → chest tube at a separate site
  C: shock + full neck veins + muffled sounds, breath sounds equal → TAMPONADE
    → eFAST subxiphoid view → pericardiocentesis as a bridge → thoracotomy / pericardial window
  Stable but widened mediastinum after deceleration → CT angiography (aortic isthmus injury)

points: **Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis**: commonest cause is positive-pressure ventilation in a patient with visceral pleural injury.

ATLS 10th moved adult needle decompression to the **4th/5th ICS just anterior to the mid-axillary line** because the chest wall at the 2nd ICS is often thicker than the needle is long; finger thoracostomy is an alternative.
Chest tube: **5th ICS (nipple level), just anterior to the mid-axillary line**, in the 'triangle of safety'; insert over the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
**Massive haemothorax** = ≥1500 mL blood (or about one-third of blood volume) in the chest; thoracotomy for ≥1500 mL immediately, >200 mL/h for 2–4 h, or persistent transfusion need.
**Open pneumothorax**: wound >2/3 the tracheal diameter lets air enter preferentially through the wound; 3-sided dressing acts as a flutter valve.
**Flail chest**: ≥2 adjacent ribs each broken in ≥2 places → paradoxical movement; the hypoxia comes mainly from the underlying **pulmonary contusion**.
**Beck triad** (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised JVP) + pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg fall in systolic BP on inspiration) = tamponade; Kussmaul sign may be present.

Blunt aortic injury is usually at the **isthmus (ligamentum arteriosum)**; CXR clues: widened mediastinum, obliterated aortic knob, trachea/NG tube deviated to the right, depressed left main bronchus, left apical cap. Confirm with CT angiography.

Lung ultrasound in eFAST: lung sliding/seashore sign = no pneumothorax at that spot; barcode (stratosphere) sign = pneumothorax; **lung point** is close to 100% specific; B-lines exclude pneumothorax at that site.
Traumatic diaphragm rupture is more often diagnosed on the **left** (the liver shields the right); NG tube in the chest on CXR is a clue.

traps.stem: Adult RTA victim, BP 70/40, absent right breath sounds, hyperresonance, trachea shifted left. Where do you decompress?
traps.trap: 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line — the classic textbook answer that many old keys still carry.
traps.fix: ATLS 10th (adult): 4th/5th ICS just anterior to the mid-axillary line. If the options offer only the 2nd ICS MCL, choose it (exam-classic, and still the site in children). Decompress before any X-ray.

traps.stem: Hypotensive trauma patient with absent left breath sounds. Tension pneumothorax or massive haemothorax?
traps.trap: Calling it tension pneumothorax because breath sounds are absent and the patient is in shock.
traps.fix: Percussion and neck veins decide it: hyperresonant + distended veins = tension pneumothorax; dull + flat veins = massive haemothorax (chest tube + blood).

traps.stem: Sucking chest wound in the field. How do you dress it?
traps.trap: Tape all four sides to make it airtight.
traps.fix: Tape only three sides (flutter valve). A fully sealed dressing can turn an open pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax; definitive care is a chest tube away from the wound.

cards.front: ATLS 10th: site for needle decompression of tension pneumothorax in an adult vs a child?
cards.back:
Adult: 4th/5th ICS just anterior to the mid-axillary line.
Child: 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line.
(2nd ICS MCL in adults = exam-classic/older answer.)

cards.text: Emergency thoracotomy for haemothorax is indicated if the chest tube drains {{c1::≥1500 mL}} immediately or more than {{c2::200 mL/h for 2–4 hours}}.
Beck triad of cardiac tamponade: {{c1::hypotension}}, {{c2::muffled heart sounds}} and {{c3::distended neck veins}}.

cards.front: Shocked trauma patient: absent breath sounds on one side, dull percussion, flat neck veins. Diagnosis and first step?
cards.back: Massive haemothorax → large-bore chest tube (5th ICS, anterior to mid-axillary line) with blood product resuscitation.

cards.text: On lung ultrasound, the {{c1::barcode (stratosphere)}} sign means no lung sliding, and the {{c2::lung point}} is the most specific sign of pneumothorax.

cards.front: Commonest site of blunt traumatic aortic injury and the best confirmatory test?
cards.back: Aortic isthmus, just distal to the left subclavian at the ligamentum arteriosum. CT angiography of the chest.

images.caption: Large left pneumothorax: no lung markings peripherally, collapsed lung edge, mediastinum and trachea pushed to the right — in a shocked patient this is tension physiology, which should be decompressed before any film is taken.

verify: ATLS 10th (2018). Exam-classic answer for adult needle decompression = 2nd ICS MCL; ATLS 10th = 4th/5th ICS anterior to mid-axillary line.

title: Haemorrhagic shock, pelvic injury & massive transfusion
subject: Surgery
anchor: Trauma + hypotension = haemorrhage until proven otherwise; look for blood 'on the floor and four more': chest, abdomen, pelvis/retroperitoneum, long bones.
Systolic BP falls only in class III (>30% loss); tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure and base deficit warn earlier.
Unstable pelvic fracture → binder over the greater trochanters; TXA within 3 h; blood products 1:1:1; permissive hypotension except in head injury.
algorithm:
Hypotensive trauma patient
  → Control external bleeding; 2 large-bore IV lines; bloods + crossmatch
  → Warm crystalloid 1 L adult (20 mL/kg child), then blood early; assess response
  → TXA 1 g IV over 10 min within 3 h of injury, then 1 g over 8 h
  → Pelvic binder at the greater trochanters if pelvic fracture suspected
  → eFAST + pelvic X-ray (adjuncts to the primary survey)
    Unstable + FAST positive → laparotomy (damage control)
    Unstable + pelvic source → binder → angioembolisation / preperitoneal packing / external fixation
    Stable → CECT abdomen/pelvis
  → Transient/non-responder → activate massive transfusion protocol (plasma:platelets:RBC ≈ 1:1:1)
  → Target SBP ~80–90 mmHg until bleeding controlled (NOT in traumatic brain injury)

tables.title: Exam-classic (ATLS 9th) version still used in many keys
head: Class
Loss (70 kg)
Heart rate
BP

points: **Shock index** = HR ÷ SBP; >1 (some use ≥0.9) suggests significant haemorrhage and predicts need for transfusion.
ATLS 10th: initial crystalloid limited to **1 L in adults (20 mL/kg in children)**; earlier ATLS used 2 L. Large-volume crystalloid worsens dilutional coagulopathy.
**TXA (CRASH-2)**: 1 g over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h, started **within 3 h** of injury; benefit is greatest when given early and it may be harmful after 3 h.
**Massive transfusion protocol**: plasma, platelets and RBC in about **1:1:1** (PROPPR: fewer deaths from exsanguination than 1:1:2). Watch for hypocalcaemia from citrate.
**Lethal triad**: hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy → damage-control surgery (stop bleeding, control contamination, close temporarily, correct in ICU, return later).
**Permissive hypotension**: accept SBP about 80–90 mmHg until haemorrhage is controlled; contraindicated in TBI, where hypotension doubles mortality.
**Pelvic binder** is centred over the **greater trochanters**, not the iliac crests; it closes an open-book (APC) injury and reduces pelvic volume.

**eFAST windows**: pericardial (subxiphoid), RUQ/hepatorenal (Morison pouch — most dependent upper-abdominal space), LUQ/splenorenal, pelvic (rectovesical/pouch of Douglas) + both anterior chest walls for pneumothorax.

**REBOA**: balloon occlusion of the aorta as a bridge to haemorrhage control — Zone I (descending thoracic, above the coeliac axis) for abdominal bleeding, Zone III (infrarenal, above the bifurcation) for pelvic bleeding.
Signs of urethral injury in pelvic fracture: blood at the meatus, perineal/scrotal haematoma, high-riding prostate → do retrograde urethrogram before a Foley catheter.

traps.stem: Trauma patient: HR 125, BP 118/90, anxious, urine output normal. Which shock class?
traps.trap: Class I because the systolic BP is normal.
traps.fix: Normal SBP does not exclude significant loss: tachycardia with narrowed pulse pressure = class II (15–30%). SBP falls only from class III.

traps.stem: Head-injured patient with GCS 7 and a bleeding splenic injury. Target systolic BP?
traps.trap: Permissive hypotension with SBP 80–90 mmHg.
traps.fix: Permissive hypotension is contraindicated in TBI. Keep SBP ≥100–110 mmHg to protect cerebral perfusion.

traps.stem: Where is a pelvic binder applied?
traps.trap: Around the iliac crests/waist, where the pelvis is felt.
traps.fix: Centred over the greater trochanters (and pubic symphysis level); a high binder does not close the pelvic ring and can splay it.

cards.text: ATLS 10th: in class III haemorrhagic shock the blood loss is {{c1::31–40%}} and the base deficit is {{c2::−6 to −10}} mEq/L.

cards.front: TXA in trauma: dose and time window (CRASH-2)?
cards.back: 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g over 8 h; start within 3 h of injury (earlier is better; late use may harm).

cards.text: Shock index = {{c1::heart rate ÷ systolic BP}}; a value above {{c2::1}} suggests significant blood loss.

cards.front: Four abdominal windows of FAST and the extra views of eFAST?
cards.back: Pericardial (subxiphoid), right upper quadrant (Morison pouch), left upper quadrant (splenorenal), pelvic. eFAST adds bilateral anterior thoracic views for pneumothorax (± haemothorax).

cards.text: A pelvic binder is centred over the {{c1::greater trochanters}}; the ratio of plasma:platelets:RBC in a massive transfusion protocol is about {{c2::1:1:1}}.

verify: ATLS 10th shock table (with base deficit) and 1 L initial crystalloid; CRASH-2 for TXA; PROPPR for 1:1:1. Older keys use the ATLS 9th HR/volume table.

title: Head injury: GCS, intracranial haematomas & herniation
subject: Surgery
anchor: Temporal blow → lucid interval → deterioration with ipsilateral dilated pupil = extradural haematoma (middle meningeal artery); biconvex on CT.
Elderly/alcoholic, minor fall, fluctuating confusion over days–weeks = chronic subdural (bridging veins); crescentic on CT, crosses sutures.
Coma out of proportion to a near-normal CT after high-speed deceleration = diffuse axonal injury (MRI SWI/GRE better).
algorithm:
Head injury
  → ABCDE; C-spine; avoid hypoxia (SpO₂ <90%) and hypotension
  → GCS + pupils (GCS-P)
    GCS ≤8 → intubate (secure airway), neurosurgical referral
  → Minor head injury (GCS 13–15 + LOC/amnesia/disorientation): apply Canadian CT Head Rule
  → NCCT head
    EDH ≥30 mL (any GCS) → craniotomy and evacuation
    Acute SDH >10 mm thick or midline shift >5 mm → evacuation
    Raised ICP → head up 30°, normocapnia (PaCO₂ 35–40), mannitol or hypertonic saline;
      brief hyperventilation only as a bridge for impending herniation

tables.title: Intracranial bleeds on CT
head: Feature
Extradural (EDH)
Acute subdural (SDH)
Subarachnoid (SAH)
Diffuse axonal injury
rows: Often normal; petechiae at grey-white junction, corpus callosum, brainstem
Usually primary brain injury; elderly, anticoagulated

points: GCS severity: **mild 13–15, moderate 9–12, severe 3–8**; 'GCS 8 — intubate'. Best motor response is the most prognostic component.
**GCS-P** = GCS minus pupil reactivity score (0 both react, 1 one unreactive, 2 both unreactive); range 1–15.

**Canadian CT Head Rule** (high risk): GCS <15 at 2 h after injury, suspected open/depressed skull fracture, any sign of basal skull fracture, ≥2 episodes of vomiting, age ≥65. Medium risk: retrograde amnesia ≥30 min, dangerous mechanism.
Basal skull fracture signs: **raccoon eyes, Battle sign** (mastoid ecchymosis), CSF rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea, haemotympanum; avoid nasal tubes.
**Cushing reflex**: hypertension (widened pulse pressure) + bradycardia + irregular respiration → late sign of raised ICP/brainstem compression.
**Monro-Kellie doctrine**: skull volume is fixed (brain + blood + CSF); a mass first displaces CSF and venous blood, then ICP rises steeply.
**Uncal (transtentorial) herniation**: ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil (CN III compression) + contralateral hemiparesis; **Kernohan notch** gives ipsilateral hemiparesis (false localising).
**Duret haemorrhages**: brainstem bleeds from downward herniation stretching pontine perforators.
EDH: pterion is the weak point overlying the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery; most EDHs are temporal/temporoparietal.
Chronic SDH: hypodense crescent after ~3 weeks; treated by burr-hole drainage when symptomatic.

traps.stem: CT: biconvex hyperdensity limited by the coronal suture after a blow to the temple. Which vessel?
traps.trap: Bridging veins — mixing up EDH and SDH.
traps.fix: Biconvex, does not cross sutures = EDH from the middle meningeal artery. Crescentic and crossing sutures = SDH from bridging veins.

traps.stem: Patient with left temporal EDH has right-sided weakness and a dilated left pupil. Later the weakness is on the left. Why?
traps.trap: A new right-sided lesion.
traps.fix: Kernohan notch phenomenon: the contralateral cerebral peduncle is compressed against the tentorium, giving ipsilateral hemiparesis (false localising). The pupil is the more reliable side marker.

traps.stem: Patient opens eyes to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds and shows decerebrate posturing. GCS?
traps.trap: Scoring decerebrate (extension) as 3.
traps.fix: E2 V2 M2 = 6. Extension (decerebrate) = M2; abnormal flexion (decorticate) = M3.

cards.text: GCS motor: {{c1::abnormal flexion (decorticate)}} scores 3 and {{c2::extension (decerebrate)}} scores 2.

cards.front: CT shape and vessel: extradural vs acute subdural haematoma?
cards.back:
EDH: biconvex/lentiform, does not cross sutures, middle meningeal artery.
SDH: crescentic, crosses sutures but not midline, bridging veins.

cards.text: Cushing reflex = {{c1::hypertension}}, {{c2::bradycardia}} and irregular respiration, a late sign of raised ICP.

cards.front: Classic signs of uncal herniation?
cards.back: Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil (CN III) + contralateral hemiparesis; declining consciousness. Kernohan notch can give ipsilateral hemiparesis.

cards.text: Canadian CT Head Rule high-risk criteria include GCS <15 at {{c1::2 hours}}, ≥2 episodes of vomiting and age ≥{{c2::65}} years.

cards.front: Deep coma after a high-speed RTA, CT shows only tiny haemorrhages at the grey-white junction and corpus callosum. Diagnosis and best imaging?
cards.back: Diffuse axonal injury; MRI with SWI/GRE sequences.

images.caption: Extradural haematoma (arrow): biconvex/lentiform hyperdensity limited by sutures, with an associated skull fracture.
Traumatic subdural haematoma: crescent-shaped collection over the convexity with mass effect and midline shift (crosses sutures, not the midline).

verify: ATLS 10th / Brain Trauma Foundation 4th ed. GCS uses 'to sound' and 'to pressure' wording (Teasdale 2014 update).

title: Burns: area, depth, fluid resuscitation & inhalation injury
subject: Surgery
anchor: Burn in a closed space + facial burns, singed nasal hair, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness = inhalation injury → early intubation.
Parkland: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA (partial + full thickness only) of Ringer lactate; half in the first 8 h counted from the TIME OF BURN.
Painless, leathery, white/charred, non-blanching = full thickness; blisters, pink, very painful, blanching = superficial partial thickness.
algorithm:
Burn patient
  → Stop the burning; cool with running water (not ice); remove clothes/jewellery
  → Airway: inhalation signs → early intubation (oedema worsens over hours)
  → Breathing: 100% O₂ if CO suspected (SpO₂ falsely normal; check COHb)
  → Estimate %TBSA (Rule of 9s adults; Lund-Browder for children; palm ≈ 1%)
  → IV fluids if >20% TBSA adult (>10–15% child) → Ringer lactate
    Parkland 4 mL/kg/%TBSA in 24 h: ½ in first 8 h from burn, ½ over next 16 h
    Children: add maintenance fluid with dextrose
  → Titrate to urine output: adult 0.5 mL/kg/h; child (<30 kg) 1 mL/kg/h; electrical with myoglobinuria ~1–1.5 mL/kg/h
  → Circumferential full-thickness burn of limb/chest with compromised circulation or ventilation → escharotomy

head: Depth
Appearance
Pain/sensation
Blanching
Healing
rows: ~1 week, no scar; not counted in %TBSA
>3 weeks; hypertrophic scar → excise and graft
White, leathery or charred; thrombosed vessels
Only from edges → excise and graft

points: **Lund-Browder chart** is the most accurate method and is preferred in children (head proportionally larger, legs smaller, changes with age).
Patient's palm including fingers ≈ **1% TBSA** — useful for small or patchy burns.
Exam-classic: **Parkland 4 mL/kg/%TBSA**. ATLS 10th starts adults at **2 mL/kg/%TBSA** (children 3 mL, electrical 4 mL) and titrates to urine output; modified Brooke also uses 2 mL.
Time for Parkland is counted **from the time of burn**, not arrival; fluid delayed by 2 h must be caught up in the remaining 6 h.
Only partial- and full-thickness burns are counted for %TBSA; erythema (superficial) is excluded.

**CO poisoning**: pulse oximeter reads falsely normal; 100% O₂ shortens COHb half-life (from ~4–5 h on air to ~1 h); consider hyperbaric O₂ in severe cases. Cyanide (burning plastics) → hydroxocobalamin.

**Electrical burns**: small skin wounds hide deep muscle damage (iceberg); ECG monitoring for arrhythmias, myoglobinuria → AKI (keep urine output high, ~100 mL/h adult until clear), compartment syndrome → fasciotomy; late cataract.

**Escharotomy** cuts through the eschar only (insensate, can be done bedside) along mid-medial/mid-lateral lines of limbs or the chest; **fasciotomy** opens the fascia for compartment syndrome (often electrical/crush).
**Curling ulcer** = stress ulcer of the stomach/duodenum after major burns (Cushing ulcer is after head injury); Marjolin ulcer = SCC in a chronic burn scar.

traps.stem: 70 kg man with 40% partial/full thickness burns arrives 2 h after injury. How much fluid in the next 6 h (Parkland)?
traps.trap: 5600 mL over 8 h counted from arrival.
traps.fix: Total 4 × 70 × 40 = 11 200 mL; half (5600 mL) is due in the first 8 h from the burn, so all 5600 mL go over the remaining 6 h; the rest over the next 16 h.

traps.stem: Child with scalds: calculate %TBSA using the adult rule of nines?
traps.trap: Using adult proportions (head 9%, each leg 18%).
traps.fix: Children have a larger head and smaller legs; use the Lund-Browder chart (infant head ≈18%, each leg ≈14%).

traps.stem: House-fire victim, alert, SpO₂ 99% on air, cherry-red appearance, headache. Next step?
traps.trap: Reassured by the normal SpO₂.
traps.fix: Pulse oximetry cannot tell COHb from oxyhaemoglobin. Give 100% O₂ by non-rebreather mask and measure COHb on ABG co-oximetry.

cards.text: Parkland formula: {{c1::4}} mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA of Ringer lactate in 24 h; half in the first {{c2::8 hours from the time of burn}}.

cards.front: Target urine output during burn resuscitation: adult, child, electrical injury?
cards.back: Adult 0.5 mL/kg/h (30–50 mL/h); child <30 kg 1 mL/kg/h; electrical injury with myoglobinuria ~1–1.5 mL/kg/h (~100 mL/h adult) until urine clears.

cards.front: Burn depth that is painless, leathery, white and does not blanch?
cards.back: Full thickness (3rd degree) — needs excision and skin grafting.

cards.text: Signs of inhalation injury: facial burns, singed {{c1::nasal hairs}}, {{c2::carbonaceous sputum}}, hoarseness and stridor → early intubation.
Escharotomy divides the {{c1::eschar}} for circumferential full-thickness burns; fasciotomy divides the {{c2::deep fascia}} for compartment syndrome.

images.caption: Wallace rule of nines (adult): head and neck 9%, each upper limb 9%, trunk 36% (front 18 + back 18), each lower limb 18%, genitalia 1%. Use Lund-Browder for children.

verify: Bailey & Love 28e; ATLS 10th (2 mL/kg/%TBSA adult start). Indian exam keys use Parkland 4 mL/kg/%TBSA.

title: Acute abdomen: appendicitis, diverticulitis & acute pancreatitis
subject: Surgery
anchor: Periumbilical pain migrating to the RIF + anorexia + fever + McBurney tenderness = appendicitis (Alvarado/MANTRELS).
Elderly, LIF pain, fever, tender mass = sigmoid diverticulitis ('left-sided appendicitis'); CT grades it (Hinchey).
Epigastric pain radiating to the back + lipase/amylase >3× ULN after alcohol or gallstones = acute pancreatitis; severity = persistent organ failure >48 h.
algorithm:
Acute pancreatitis (2 of 3: typical pain, lipase/amylase >3× ULN, imaging)
  → No CT on day 1 if diagnosis is clear (CT if diagnosis doubtful or no improvement)
  → Goal-directed fluids (Ringer lactate; avoid aggressive overload), analgesia, early oral/enteral feeding
  → Severity: BISAP ≥3 / persistent SIRS → HDU/ICU; organ failure >48 h = severe
  → Gallstone pancreatitis + cholangitis → ERCP within 24 h; cholecystectomy in the same admission (mild)
  → CECT after 72 h (or 5–7 days) to assess necrosis
  → Infected necrosis (gas in collection, sepsis) → antibiotics (carbapenem) → STEP-UP:
      percutaneous/endoscopic drainage → minimally invasive necrosectomy if no response
      delay intervention ≥4 weeks until walled-off necrosis forms

tables.title: Revised Atlanta 2012: severity and collections
head: Item
Definition
rows: No organ failure, no local or systemic complications
Transient organ failure (<48 h) and/or local or systemic complications
Persistent organ failure >48 h (modified Marshall score ≥2)
<4 weeks: acute peripancreatic fluid collection (APFC) → >4 weeks: pseudocyst (well-defined wall, no solid debris)
<4 weeks: acute necrotic collection (ANC) → >4 weeks: walled-off necrosis (WON)

tables.title: Scores at a glance
head: Score
Components
Cut-off
rows: Migration of pain 1, Anorexia 1, Nausea/vomiting 1, Tenderness RIF 2, Rebound 1, Elevated temp 1, Leucocytosis 2, Shift to left 1
Age, sex, clinical signs, WBC, urine; designed for Asian populations
I pericolic abscess; II pelvic/distant abscess; III purulent peritonitis; IV faecal peritonitis
I–II antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage; III–IV surgery
BUN >25 mg/dL, Impaired mental status, SIRS, Age >60, Pleural effusion
Admission: age >55, WBC >16 000, glucose >200, LDH >350, AST >250. At 48 h: Hct fall >10%, BUN rise >5, Ca <8, PaO₂ <60, base deficit >4, fluid sequestration >6 L

points: **Lipase** is more specific and stays elevated longer than amylase; the level does not correlate with severity.
**CECT is best done after 72 h**: necrosis is under-estimated earlier. Early CT only if the diagnosis is uncertain.

Commonest causes of acute pancreatitis: **gallstones** (overall) and **alcohol**; others — hypertriglyceridaemia (>1000 mg/dL), hypercalcaemia, post-ERCP, drugs (azathioprine, valproate), scorpion sting.
**Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended** in sterile necrosis; give them for proven/suspected infected necrosis (gas bubbles on CT).
**Step-up approach** (PANTER): drainage first, necrosectomy only if needed, ideally **after 4 weeks** when the collection is walled off.
Pseudocyst: drain only if symptomatic/complicated (endoscopic cystogastrostomy preferred); size alone (>6 cm) is the old indication.
Cullen sign (periumbilical) and Grey Turner sign (flank) ecchymosis = retroperitoneal haemorrhage in severe pancreatitis.

Appendicitis: **McBurney point** (lateral 1/3 of spinous-umbilical line), Rovsing, psoas (retrocaecal), obturator (pelvic) signs; CT is most accurate in adults, ultrasound first in children and pregnancy.
Appendicular mass (lump) → conservative **Ochsner-Sherren** regime; abscess → percutaneous drainage; interval appendicectomy is optional.
Diverticulitis: **CT abdomen** is investigation of choice; avoid colonoscopy and barium enema in the acute phase (perforation risk); colonoscopy at ~6 weeks to exclude cancer.

traps.stem: Acute pancreatitis, day 1, diagnosis clear on pain and lipase. Next step to assess severity?
traps.trap: Urgent contrast CT abdomen.
traps.fix: CT is not needed for diagnosis when pain + enzymes are typical, and necrosis is underestimated before 72 h. Assess severity clinically (SIRS, BISAP, organ failure); CECT after 72 h if not improving.

traps.stem: Infected walled-off pancreatic necrosis on day 10, patient stable on antibiotics. Next step?
traps.trap: Immediate open necrosectomy.
traps.fix: Step-up approach: continue antibiotics, delay; percutaneous or endoscopic drainage first, minimally invasive necrosectomy if no response, ideally after 4 weeks.

traps.stem: Severe pancreatitis defined in Revised Atlanta by?
traps.trap: Ranson ≥3 or presence of necrosis on CT.
traps.fix: Persistent organ failure >48 h. Transient organ failure or local complications only = moderately severe.

cards.text: Revised Atlanta: severe acute pancreatitis = persistent organ failure lasting more than {{c1::48 hours}}; a peripancreatic collection becomes a pseudocyst or WON after {{c2::4 weeks}}.

cards.front: Components of BISAP score?
cards.back: BUN >25 mg/dL, Impaired mental status, SIRS, Age >60, Pleural effusion. Score ≥3 = high risk.

cards.front: Timing of CECT in acute pancreatitis and why?
cards.back: After 72 h (often 5–7 days) — earlier scans underestimate necrosis; early CT only if diagnosis is in doubt.

cards.text: Alvarado score: the two items scoring 2 points are {{c1::right iliac fossa tenderness}} and {{c2::leucocytosis}}; total = 10.
Hinchey stage {{c1::III}} = purulent peritonitis and stage {{c2::IV}} = faecal peritonitis.

cards.front: Management sequence for infected pancreatic necrosis?
cards.back: Antibiotics (e.g. carbapenem) → delay → step-up: percutaneous/endoscopic drainage → minimally invasive necrosectomy, ideally after 4 weeks (walled-off).

verify: Revised Atlanta 2012; IAP/APA 2013 and AGA guidance; Bailey & Love 28e. RIPASA cut-off 7.5.

title: Intestinal obstruction, volvulus, intussusception & mesenteric ischaemia
subject: Surgery
anchor: Colicky pain, vomiting, distension, absolute constipation = obstruction; early vomiting = proximal small bowel, early distension = large bowel.
Elderly, chronically constipated, massive distension, 'coffee bean' loop rising from the pelvis to the RUQ = sigmoid volvulus.
AF patient with severe abdominal pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen + rising lactate = acute mesenteric ischaemia → CT angiography.
algorithm:
Suspected obstruction
  → Erect/supine X-ray → CECT abdomen (cause, level, closed loop, ischaemia)
  → Strangulation signs (fever, tachycardia, constant pain, peritonism, ↑lactate) → urgent surgery
  → Adhesive SBO without strangulation → drip and suck ± water-soluble contrast
      (contrast in colon by 24 h predicts resolution)
  → Sigmoid volvulus, no gangrene → flexible sigmoidoscopic detorsion + flatus tube
      → elective sigmoid colectomy later (high recurrence)
      gangrene/perforation → Hartmann procedure
  → Caecal volvulus → right hemicolectomy (endoscopic detorsion rarely works)
  → Acute mesenteric ischaemia → heparin + resuscitation → CTA →
      embolectomy/bypass + resect dead bowel + second-look laparotomy

points: **3-6-9 rule**: upper limit of normal diameter — small bowel 3 cm, colon 6 cm, caecum 9 cm.
**Closed-loop obstruction** (volvulus, LBO with competent ileocaecal valve) risks caecal perforation; caecum >12 cm is a danger sign.

**Intussusception**: 6 months–3 years (mostly ileocolic), colicky pain with drawing up of legs, **red-currant-jelly stool**, sausage-shaped mass, empty RIF (**Dance sign**); USG shows **target/doughnut** (transverse) and **pseudokidney** (longitudinal) signs.

Intussusception treatment: **pneumatic or hydrostatic reduction** under image guidance; surgery if peritonitis, perforation or shock, or failed reduction. In adults, a lead point (often tumour) → resection.

**Acute mesenteric ischaemia**: SMA embolism (usually from AF) is commonest; embolus lodges beyond the middle colic origin, so proximal jejunum is spared. Thrombosis affects the SMA origin (atherosclerotic, prior intestinal angina).
Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (low-flow, vasopressors, digoxin) → catheter angiography with intra-arterial papaverine.
**Gallstone ileus**: Rigler triad = pneumobilia + SBO + ectopic gallstone; stone usually impacts at the **terminal ileum**; treat by enterolithotomy.
**Ogilvie syndrome** (acute colonic pseudo-obstruction): massive colonic dilatation without mechanical cause → IV **neostigmine** if caecum >10–12 cm despite conservative care.
Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) is both diagnostic and possibly therapeutic in adhesive SBO.
Strangulation is most likely with femoral hernia and closed-loop obstruction; it does not always show peritonism early — lactate and CT signs help.

traps.stem: Elderly man, sigmoid volvulus, no peritonitis, successful sigmoidoscopic detorsion. Further plan?
traps.trap: Discharge after detorsion — problem solved.
traps.fix: Recurrence is high (about half); plan elective sigmoid colectomy in the same admission if fit.

traps.stem: 30-year-old with caecal volvulus. Treatment?
traps.trap: Colonoscopic detorsion as for sigmoid volvulus.
traps.fix: Endoscopic detorsion is rarely successful and risky in caecal volvulus; right hemicolectomy (ileocolic resection) is the treatment.

traps.stem: Patient with AF has severe abdominal pain; examination is soft with minimal tenderness. Most likely?
traps.trap: Non-specific abdominal pain or gastritis because signs are minimal.
traps.fix: Pain out of proportion to signs = acute mesenteric ischaemia until proven otherwise; CT angiography is the investigation of choice.

cards.front: X-ray feature distinguishing small from large bowel loops?
cards.back: Small bowel: central, valvulae conniventes cross the full width. Large bowel: peripheral, haustra cross only part of the width.

cards.text: Sigmoid volvulus: X-ray shows the {{c1::coffee bean (bent inner tube)}} sign; first-line treatment is {{c2::flexible sigmoidoscopic detorsion with a flatus tube}}.
Intussusception on ultrasound: {{c1::target (doughnut)}} sign in transverse section and {{c2::pseudokidney}} sign in longitudinal section.

cards.front: Investigation of choice for acute mesenteric ischaemia?
cards.back: CT angiography (multidetector CTA). Lactate rises late; plain X-ray is often normal early.

cards.text: Rigler triad of gallstone ileus: {{c1::pneumobilia}}, small bowel obstruction and an {{c2::ectopic gallstone}}, usually at the terminal ileum.

title: Upper GI: achalasia, GERD/Barrett, peptic ulcer, bariatrics, ZES & GOO
subject: Surgery
anchor: Dysphagia to solids AND liquids from the start + regurgitation + bird-beak on barium = achalasia; confirm with high-resolution manometry.
Sudden severe epigastric pain → board-like rigidity + free gas under the diaphragm on erect CXR = perforated peptic ulcer.
Long-standing ulcer + projectile non-bilious vomiting of old food + succussion splash = gastric outlet obstruction → hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.
algorithm:
Dysphagia to solids and liquids
  → Endoscopy first (exclude pseudo-achalasia / GEJ cancer)
  → Barium swallow (bird-beak, dilated oesophagus)
  → High-resolution manometry (gold standard): raised IRP + absent peristalsis
    Type II → best response to any therapy (pneumatic dilatation, Heller, POEM)
    Type III (spastic) → POEM preferred (longer myotomy)
    Unfit → botulinum toxin
Gastric outlet obstruction
  → NG aspiration, IV 0.9% saline + KCl (correct alkalosis and hypokalaemia first)
  → Endoscopy + biopsy (exclude malignancy) → dilatation or surgery

points: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory (NO/VIP) neurons of the **myenteric plexus**; Chagas disease (T. cruzi) causes secondary achalasia; long-term risk of **squamous cell carcinoma**.
**Heller myotomy + partial fundoplication (Dor/Toupet)** or **POEM**; POEM has more post-procedure reflux than Heller + Dor.
**Barrett oesophagus**: columnar metaplasia with **goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia)** ≥1 cm above the GEJ → risk of adenocarcinoma; dysplasia → endoscopic resection + radiofrequency ablation.
**Nissen fundoplication** = 360° posterior wrap for refractory GERD; manometry before surgery to exclude achalasia/aperistalsis.

Perforated ulcer: commonest is **anterior duodenal**; erect CXR free gas is missed in a proportion, so **CT** is more sensitive; treatment = resuscitation + **Graham omental patch**, then H. pylori eradication.
Bleeding **posterior duodenal ulcer** erodes the **gastroduodenal artery**; gastric ulcer on lesser curve → left gastric artery.

**Zollinger-Ellison**: gastrinoma (duodenum commonest site; ~25% MEN1), multiple/distal duodenal or jejunal ulcers + diarrhoea; fasting gastrin >10× ULN with gastric pH <2 is diagnostic; **secretin test** paradoxically raises gastrin. Gastrinoma triangle: cystic–CBD junction, 2nd/3rd part of duodenum, neck/body of pancreas.
**GOO metabolic picture**: loss of HCl → hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; kidney conserves Na⁺ by excreting K⁺ and later H⁺ → **paradoxical aciduria**. Correct with **0.9% saline + KCl**.

Bariatric surgery indication (classic NIH): BMI ≥40, or ≥35 with comorbidity; Asian/Indian cut-offs are lower (≈ BMI ≥37.5, or ≥32.5 with comorbidity); ASMBS/IFSO 2022 lowered thresholds further (≥35 regardless; consider ≥30 with metabolic disease).

traps.stem: 60-year-old with 3 months of progressive dysphagia and weight loss; barium shows bird-beak narrowing. Next step?
traps.trap: Manometry and pneumatic dilatation for achalasia.
traps.fix: Short history, older age and weight loss suggest pseudo-achalasia from GEJ cancer; do endoscopy (± EUS/CT) first.

traps.stem: Pyloric obstruction from chronic ulcer: urine is acidic despite metabolic alkalosis. Why?
traps.trap: Coexisting renal tubular acidosis.
traps.fix: Paradoxical aciduria: with volume, Cl⁻ and K⁺ depletion the distal nephron reabsorbs Na⁺ in exchange for H⁺ (and K⁺). Treat with normal saline + KCl.

traps.stem: Which achalasia subtype responds best to treatment?
traps.trap: Type I (classic), because it is the 'typical' form.
traps.fix: Type II (pan-oesophageal pressurisation) responds best; type III (spastic) does worst with dilatation and is best treated by POEM.

cards.text: Achalasia: manometry shows {{c1::incomplete LES relaxation (raised IRP)}} with {{c2::absent peristalsis}}; type {{c3::II}} has the best prognosis.

cards.front: Metabolic picture of gastric outlet obstruction and its correction?
cards.back: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Correct with IV 0.9% NaCl + KCl.

cards.text: Bleeding posterior duodenal ulcer erodes the {{c1::gastroduodenal artery}}; perforated anterior duodenal ulcer is repaired with a {{c2::Graham omental patch}}.

cards.front: Diagnostic test for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome when gastrin is equivocal?
cards.back: Secretin stimulation test — gastrin rises paradoxically in gastrinoma (falls or no change normally).

cards.text: Barrett oesophagus is defined by {{c1::intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells}} in the distal oesophagus and predisposes to {{c2::adenocarcinoma}}.

title: GI malignancy: oesophagus, stomach, colorectum, anal canal, carcinoid
subject: Surgery
anchor: Smoker/drinker, mid-oesophagus, progressive dysphagia = SCC; obese man with GERD/Barrett, lower oesophagus = adenocarcinoma.
Young patient, signet-ring cells, leather-bottle stomach, CDH1 = diffuse (Lauren) gastric cancer; elderly, H. pylori, distal glandular tumour = intestinal type.
Right colon cancer → anaemia and mass; left colon → altered bowel habit, obstruction, apple-core lesion on barium.
algorithm:
Rectal cancer
  → Colonoscopy + biopsy; CEA; CT chest-abdomen-pelvis; pelvic MRI (local stage, CRM)
  → Early (T1–T2, N0) → surgery with TME (low anterior resection; APR if sphincter involved)
  → Locally advanced (T3–T4 or N+, threatened CRM) → neoadjuvant chemoradiation / total neoadjuvant therapy → TME
Colon cancer
  → Resection with ≥12 nodes → stage III (N+) → adjuvant FOLFOX/CAPOX
Anal canal SCC
  → Nigro protocol: chemoradiation (5-FU + mitomycin C + RT) first-line
  → APR only for residual/recurrent disease

tables.title: Gastric cancer: Lauren classification
head: Feature
Intestinal type
Diffuse type
rows: Signet-ring cells, no glands, linitis plastica
H. pylori, atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, diet
CDH1 (E-cadherin) germline mutation, blood group A

points: Gastric cancer surgery: **D2 lymphadenectomy** is the standard with gastrectomy; T1a mucosal lesions may be treated by endoscopic resection (EMR/ESD).

Signs of spread in gastric cancer: **Virchow node** (left supraclavicular, Troisier sign), **Sister Mary Joseph nodule** (umbilicus), **Blumer shelf** (rectovesical/rectouterine pouch), **Irish node** (left axilla), Krukenberg tumour.
Colorectal T stage: T1 submucosa, T2 muscularis propria, T3 through muscularis into pericolorectal tissue, T4a visceral peritoneum, T4b other organs; N1 = 1–3 nodes, N2 = ≥4.
**Total mesorectal excision (Heald)** removes the rectum with its intact mesorectal envelope → lowers local recurrence; circumferential resection margin >1 mm.

**MSI-H/dMMR** tumours: right-sided, mucinous, lymphocytic infiltrate, better stage-for-stage prognosis, respond to **immune checkpoint inhibitors** (pembrolizumab); ~15% of sporadic CRC (mostly MLH1 promoter hypermethylation).
**Lynch syndrome**: germline MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 (or EPCAM); **Amsterdam II 3-2-1** rule; commonest extracolonic cancer = **endometrium**.

**FAP**: APC gene on **5q21**, >100 adenomas, near-100% cancer risk → restorative proctocolectomy with **ileal pouch-anal anastomosis**; CHRPE; Gardner (osteomas, desmoids), Turcot (brain tumours). Leading causes of death after colectomy: periampullary/duodenal cancer and desmoids.
**Anal canal**: SCC (HPV 16, HIV, receptive anal intercourse); below the dentate line drains to **superficial inguinal nodes**. Nigro protocol = 5-FU + mitomycin C + radiotherapy.
**Carcinoid (NET)**: commonest in small intestine (ileum) and appendix; appendiceal NET <2 cm at the tip → appendicectomy; >2 cm or base/mesoappendix involvement → right hemicolectomy.

**Carcinoid syndrome** (flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, right-sided valve disease — tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary stenosis) needs **liver metastases**; diagnose with urinary **5-HIAA**; treat with octreotide; niacin deficiency (pellagra) possible.

traps.stem: Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal, T2N0. First-line treatment?
traps.trap: Abdominoperineal resection, as for low rectal adenocarcinoma.
traps.fix: Nigro protocol chemoradiation (5-FU + mitomycin C + RT) preserves the sphincter; APR is salvage for persistent/recurrent disease.

traps.stem: Appendicectomy specimen shows a 2.5 cm carcinoid at the base of the appendix. Next step?
traps.trap: Nothing further; appendicectomy is curative for carcinoid.
traps.fix: Size >2 cm or base/mesoappendix involvement → right hemicolectomy. Simple appendicectomy is enough only for small (<2 cm) tip lesions.

traps.stem: Carcinoid of the ileum without liver metastasis. Will the patient have flushing and diarrhoea?
traps.trap: Yes — all midgut carcinoids cause carcinoid syndrome.
traps.fix: Serotonin is inactivated by the liver; carcinoid syndrome usually needs hepatic metastases (or primary draining outside the portal system, e.g. bronchial/ovarian).

cards.front: Lauren diffuse gastric cancer: histology, gene and spread?
cards.back: Signet-ring cells without glands (linitis plastica); germline CDH1 (E-cadherin) in hereditary form; transmural and peritoneal spread (Krukenberg).

cards.text: Nigro protocol for anal canal SCC = {{c1::5-FU}} + {{c2::mitomycin C}} + radiotherapy.
Commonest extracolonic cancer in Lynch syndrome is {{c1::endometrial carcinoma}}; FAP is caused by {{c2::APC}} gene mutation on chromosome 5q21.

cards.front: Investigation and marker for carcinoid syndrome?
cards.back: 24-h urinary 5-HIAA (and serum chromogranin A); somatostatin receptor imaging (Ga-68 DOTATATE PET) for localisation.

cards.text: In rectal cancer, {{c1::total mesorectal excision}} reduces local recurrence; locally advanced tumours (T3/T4 or N+) receive {{c2::neoadjuvant chemoradiation}} first.

title: Hepatobiliary: gallstones, cholangitis, choledochal cyst, liver lesions, Whipple
subject: Surgery
anchor: Fever with rigors + RUQ pain + jaundice = Charcot triad (acute cholangitis); add hypotension + confusion = Reynolds pentad → urgent biliary drainage (ERCP).
Painless progressive jaundice + palpable non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier) ± weight loss = periampullary/pancreatic head cancer → Whipple if resectable.
Infant with persistent jaundice beyond 2 weeks, pale stools, dark urine = biliary atresia → Kasai portoenterostomy, best before 60 days.
algorithm:
Acute cholangitis (Tokyo 2018)
  → Blood cultures, IV antibiotics, fluids
  → Grade III (organ dysfunction) → urgent biliary drainage (ERCP) after resuscitation
  → Grade II (moderate) → early drainage (within 24–48 h)
  → Grade I (mild) → antibiotics; drain if no response
  → Interval cholecystectomy for stones
Acute calculous cholecystitis
  → Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 h–7 days of onset), not interval surgery, if fit
Periampullary mass
  → CECT pancreas protocol → resectable → pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple)
    (no routine preoperative biliary stenting unless cholangitis or delayed surgery)

points: **Tokyo 2018 cholangitis severity**: III = any organ dysfunction; II = two of WBC >12 000 or <4000, fever ≥39 °C, age ≥75, bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL, low albumin; I = neither.

**Biliary atresia**: triangular cord sign on USG, no excretion on HIDA, **intraoperative cholangiogram** confirms; **Kasai** portoenterostomy best within **60 days**; failure → liver transplant (commonest indication in children).
**Klatskin tumour** (hilar cholangiocarcinoma) — **Bismuth-Corlette**: I below confluence, II at confluence, IIIa extends into right hepatic duct, IIIb into left, IV both sides/multifocal.

**Hydatid cyst** (E. granulosus): 'water-lily' sign (detached membranes), daughter cysts; **PAIR** (puncture, aspiration, injection of scolicide, re-aspiration) under albendazole cover — contraindicated when the cyst communicates with the biliary tree; avoid formalin as scolicide in that case (sclerosing cholangitis).

**Gallbladder cancer**: commonest in north India; risk — gallstones, **porcelain gallbladder**, anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction, choledochal cyst; T1a → simple cholecystectomy; **T1b and beyond → extended cholecystectomy** (segments IVb/V + lymphadenectomy).
**Couinaud**: 8 functional segments based on portal and hepatic vein branches; **segment I (caudate)** drains directly into the IVC, so it hypertrophies in Budd-Chiari.

Whipple (pancreaticoduodenectomy) removes pancreatic head, duodenum, distal CBD, gallbladder ± distal stomach; commonest serious complication = **pancreatic fistula**; delayed gastric emptying is the commonest overall.
Ampullary carcinoma: intermittent jaundice, **silver stool** (bleeding + acholic stool), best prognosis among periampullary cancers.
**Mirizzi syndrome**: stone in Hartmann pouch/cystic duct compresses the CHD → obstructive jaundice; Csendes classification.
Investigation of choice for gallstones = **USG**; for CBD stones without intervention = **MRCP**; ERCP is therapeutic.

traps.stem: Fever, jaundice, RUQ pain, BP 80/50 and confusion. Most important step after resuscitation and antibiotics?
traps.trap: Urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
traps.fix: Reynolds pentad = Tokyo grade III cholangitis → urgent biliary decompression, preferably ERCP (PTBD if ERCP fails). Cholecystectomy later.

traps.stem: Choledochal cyst type I. Best operation?
traps.trap: Cystoduodenostomy/cystojejunostomy (internal drainage).
traps.fix: Complete cyst excision with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy; internal drainage leaves the cyst wall with high cholangiocarcinoma and cholangitis risk.

traps.stem: Hydatid liver cyst with bile-stained aspirate. Proceed with PAIR?
traps.trap: Yes — inject hypertonic saline/alcohol as usual.
traps.fix: Bile in the cyst = cysto-biliary communication: PAIR is contraindicated (risk of chemical sclerosing cholangitis). Treat surgically/endoscopically under albendazole cover.

cards.text: Charcot triad = fever, {{c1::RUQ pain}} and jaundice; Reynolds pentad adds {{c2::hypotension}} and {{c3::altered mental status}}.

cards.front: Commonest Todani type and its treatment?
cards.back: Type I (fusiform/cystic extrahepatic CBD dilatation) → complete excision + Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy.

cards.text: Kasai portoenterostomy for biliary atresia gives the best results when done before {{c1::60 days}} of age.

cards.front: Bismuth-Corlette type IIIa vs IIIb?
cards.back: IIIa: hilar tumour extends into the right hepatic duct; IIIb: into the left hepatic duct. IV: both sides or multifocal.

cards.text: In Couinaud anatomy, segment {{c1::I (caudate lobe)}} drains directly into the IVC and enlarges in {{c2::Budd-Chiari syndrome}}.

cards.front: Gallbladder cancer found to be T1b after cholecystectomy. Next step?
cards.back: Re-operate for extended (radical) cholecystectomy: resection of liver bed (segments IVb/V) + regional lymphadenectomy. T1a needs only simple cholecystectomy.

title: Thyroid nodule & cancer; breast cancer workup and subtypes
subject: Surgery
anchor: Thyroid nodule workup = TSH → ultrasound → FNAC reported in Bethesda I–VI; low TSH → radionuclide scan first (hot nodule rarely malignant).
Young woman, radiation history, cervical node, Orphan Annie nuclei + psammoma bodies = papillary carcinoma; calcitonin + amyloid stroma + MEN2/RET = medullary.
Breast lump workup = triple assessment: clinical exam + imaging (mammogram ≥35–40 y / USG if younger) + core-needle biopsy.
algorithm:
Thyroid nodule
  → TSH
    Low → radionuclide scan → hot nodule: treat hyperthyroidism (FNA usually not needed)
    Normal/high → USG neck → FNAC if suspicious features/size criteria
  → Bethesda I: repeat USG-guided FNA
    II: follow-up
    III (AUS): repeat FNA / molecular testing / lobectomy
    IV (follicular neoplasm): molecular testing or diagnostic lobectomy
    V: lobectomy or total thyroidectomy
    VI: surgery (lobectomy for low-risk 1–4 cm PTC; total thyroidectomy for >4 cm, nodes, extrathyroidal extension)
Breast lump
  → Triple assessment → core biopsy with ER/PR/HER2/Ki-67
  → Clinically node-negative → sentinel node biopsy; node-positive → axillary dissection (or neoadjuvant then re-stage)

points: **Bethesda (TBSRTC)**: I non-diagnostic, II benign, III atypia of undetermined significance, IV follicular neoplasm, V suspicious for malignancy, VI malignant.
Follicular carcinoma vs adenoma needs **capsular/vascular invasion on histology** → FNAC can only say 'follicular neoplasm' (Bethesda IV).

**Recurrent laryngeal nerve**: unilateral injury → hoarseness; bilateral → stridor/airway obstruction (cords in paramedian position) → tracheostomy. **External branch of superior laryngeal nerve** (with superior thyroid artery) → loss of high-pitched voice, voice fatigue.
**Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia** (parathyroid injury/devascularisation): perioral tingling, **Chvostek** and **Trousseau** signs, usually 24–72 h → IV calcium gluconate.
Other early complications: **haematoma causing airway compromise** → open the wound at the bedside; thyroid storm.
**MTC**: prophylactic total thyroidectomy in RET carriers (age by risk level — earliest in MEN2B, within the first year of life); exclude **phaeochromocytoma** before surgery.
**BI-RADS**: 0 incomplete, 1 negative, 2 benign, 3 probably benign (<2% malignancy, short-interval follow-up), 4 suspicious (biopsy), 5 highly suggestive (≥95%), 6 known biopsy-proven cancer.
**Sentinel node biopsy**: blue dye (isosulfan/methylene blue) ± Tc-99m sulfur colloid; standard for clinically node-negative early breast cancer; contraindicated in **inflammatory breast cancer**.

**Phyllodes tumour vs fibroadenoma**: phyllodes in older women (40s), rapidly growing, large, leaf-like stromal overgrowth → **wide local excision with ≥1 cm margin**, no axillary dissection (spreads haematogenously). Fibroadenoma: young, mobile 'breast mouse', reassure/excise.

Breast-conserving surgery + radiotherapy is equivalent to mastectomy for suitable early cancers; contraindications include multicentric disease, inability to get radiotherapy, and diffuse malignant microcalcifications.

traps.stem: FNAC of a thyroid nodule reports 'follicular neoplasm'. Can it be called follicular carcinoma?
traps.trap: Yes — cytology shows follicular malignant cells.
traps.fix: No. Follicular carcinoma needs capsular/vascular invasion on histology; Bethesda IV → molecular testing or diagnostic lobectomy.

traps.stem: Opera singer after thyroidectomy can no longer reach high notes; voice tires easily. Which nerve?
traps.trap: Recurrent laryngeal nerve.
traps.fix: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (supplies cricothyroid), at risk while ligating the superior thyroid pedicle. RLN injury → hoarseness or stridor.

traps.stem: 45-year-old woman with a rapidly enlarging 8 cm well-circumscribed breast mass; core biopsy shows leaf-like stromal overgrowth. Surgery?
traps.trap: Mastectomy with axillary clearance as for carcinoma.
traps.fix: Phyllodes tumour → wide local excision with ≥1 cm margins; axillary dissection not needed as nodal spread is rare.

cards.back: I non-diagnostic; II benign; III atypia of undetermined significance; IV follicular neoplasm; V suspicious for malignancy; VI malignant.

cards.text: Medullary carcinoma thyroid arises from {{c1::parafollicular C cells}}, secretes {{c2::calcitonin}} and is linked to {{c3::RET}} mutations (MEN 2).

cards.front: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy after thyroidectomy: presentation and management?
cards.back: Stridor and respiratory distress soon after extubation (cords near midline); needs re-intubation/tracheostomy.

cards.front: Phyllodes tumour vs fibroadenoma: age, growth, treatment?
cards.back: Phyllodes: 40s, rapid growth, large, leaf-like stroma → wide excision ≥1 cm margin, no axillary surgery. Fibroadenoma: teens–20s, slow, mobile; observe or simple excision.

title: Vascular: limb ischaemia, PAD, aortic disease, DVT & varicose veins
subject: Surgery
anchor: Sudden cold, pale, painful leg in a patient with AF = acute embolic limb ischaemia (6 Ps); sensory/motor loss = threatened limb → urgent revascularisation.
Tearing chest pain radiating to the back + BP difference between arms + widened mediastinum = aortic dissection; ascending (Stanford A) = surgery.
Calf pain on walking relieved by rest = claudication; ABI <0.9 confirms PAD; rest pain/ulcer = chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.
algorithm:
Acute limb ischaemia
  → IV heparin bolus immediately
  → Rutherford class
    I (viable) → imaging (CTA/duplex) → planned revascularisation
    IIa (marginally threatened) → prompt revascularisation (catheter thrombolysis or surgery)
    IIb (immediately threatened) → emergency embolectomy/bypass
    III (irreversible) → primary amputation
  → Fasciotomy if reperfusion compartment syndrome
Aortic dissection
  → IV β-blocker (esmolol/labetalol): HR <60, SBP 100–120 → CTA
    Stanford A (ascending) → emergency open surgery
    Stanford B (descending) → medical; TEVAR if complicated (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain/HTN)

points: **6 Ps**: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishing cold (poikilothermia); paraesthesia and paralysis mark a threatened limb.
**ABI**: normal 1.0–1.4; <0.9 = PAD; <0.4 = severe/critical; **>1.4 = non-compressible calcified vessels** (diabetes, CKD — Mönckeberg) → use toe-brachial index.

**Embolus vs thrombosis**: embolus — sudden, AF/recent MI, normal contralateral pulses, commonest at the **common femoral bifurcation**; thrombosis — prior claudication, absent contralateral pulses, collaterals.
**AAA**: elective repair at **≥5.5 cm** in men (≥5.0 cm in women per ESVS), growth >1 cm/year, or symptoms; commonest site infrarenal; screening men ≥65 by ultrasound.

**Stanford A** involves the ascending aorta (DeBakey I & II) → surgery; **Stanford B** spares it (DeBakey III) → medical BP/HR control, TEVAR if complicated. CTA is the investigation of choice (TEE if unstable).

**DVT prophylaxis**: early mobilisation, graduated compression/intermittent pneumatic compression, LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily) according to Caprini risk; Virchow triad = stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability.

**Varicose veins**: commonest cause is **saphenofemoral junction** incompetence (GSV); duplex ultrasound is the investigation of choice; endovenous ablation (laser/RFA) is now first-line over high ligation and stripping.

**Trendelenburg test** (Brodie-Trendelenburg): tests SFJ/GSV valve competence; **Perthes test**: tests deep vein patency (pain/engorgement on walking with tourniquet = deep vein obstruction → avoid superficial vein surgery).
**CEAP 'C'**: C0 none, C1 telangiectasia/reticular, C2 varicose veins, C3 oedema, C4 skin changes (pigmentation, eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche), C5 healed ulcer, C6 active ulcer.
Venous ulcer: gaiter area (medial malleolus), treated with **multilayer compression** after confirming ABI >0.8; arterial ulcer: toes/pressure points, punched out, painful.

traps.stem: Diabetic with non-healing toe ulcer and absent pedal pulses has ABI 1.5. Interpretation?
traps.trap: Normal — no PAD.
traps.fix: ABI >1.4 = non-compressible calcified arteries; it is falsely high. Use toe-brachial index or duplex to assess PAD.

traps.stem: Acute limb ischaemia with sensory loss beyond the toes and mild weakness, arterial Doppler inaudible, venous audible. Class and action?
traps.trap: Class III → amputation because there is motor weakness.
traps.fix: Rutherford IIb (immediately threatened) → emergency revascularisation. Class III needs profound anaesthesia, paralysis and inaudible venous signals.

traps.stem: Type B aortic dissection, pain controlled, no malperfusion. Treatment?
traps.trap: Emergency open surgical repair like type A.
traps.fix: Uncomplicated type B → medical therapy (IV β-blocker first, target HR <60 and SBP 100–120). TEVAR for complicated type B.

cards.text: ABI below {{c1::0.9}} indicates PAD; above {{c2::1.4}} suggests non-compressible calcified vessels.

cards.front: Rutherford acute limb ischaemia class III: findings and management?
cards.back: Profound sensory loss, paralysis/rigor, inaudible arterial AND venous Doppler → irreversible → primary amputation.

cards.text: Stanford type {{c1::A}} dissection involves the ascending aorta and needs surgery; type {{c2::B}} is managed medically unless complicated (TEVAR).

cards.front: Elective repair threshold for an asymptomatic AAA?
cards.back: Diameter ≥5.5 cm in men (≥5.0 cm in women, ESVS), or growth >1 cm/year, or symptoms.

cards.text: The {{c1::Perthes}} test assesses deep vein patency, while the {{c2::Trendelenburg}} test assesses saphenofemoral junction competence.

title: Urology: stones, renal & testicular tumours, torsion, BPH, bladder cancer, PUV
subject: Surgery
anchor: Loin-to-groin colic + haematuria = ureteric stone → NCCT KUB (investigation of choice).
Adolescent with sudden severe testicular pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex = torsion → surgical exploration without waiting for imaging.
Male infant with poor stream, palpable bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis (antenatal oligohydramnios) = posterior urethral valves → VCUG.
algorithm:
Renal/ureteric stone (confirmed on NCCT KUB)
  → Analgesia (NSAID first-line)
  → Obstructed + infected kidney → urgent decompression (DJ stent or PCN) + antibiotics; stone later
  → Distal ureteric stone ≤10 mm → medical expulsive therapy (tamsulosin)
  → Ureteric stone not passing → URS (or ESWL for proximal)
  → Renal stone <10 mm → ESWL or RIRS
    10–20 mm → ESWL or endourology (lower pole: PCNL/RIRS)
    >20 mm or staghorn → PCNL
Suspected torsion
  → Immediate scrotal exploration → detorsion + bilateral orchidopexy (orchidectomy if non-viable)

points: Stones: **calcium oxalate** commonest; **struvite** (Mg-NH₄-PO₄) from urease organisms (Proteus) → staghorn, coffin-lid crystals; **uric acid** radiolucent on X-ray (seen on CT), dissolved by urinary alkalinisation; **cystine** hexagonal crystals, faintly radiopaque.

ESWL contraindications: **pregnancy**, uncorrected bleeding disorder, untreated UTI, distal obstruction, aortic aneurysm near the stone; less effective for cystine, calcium oxalate monohydrate and dense stones (>1000 HU).

**RCC**: clear-cell (VHL, chromosome 3p) commonest; classic triad (haematuria, flank pain, mass) seen in a minority. Paraneoplastic: **polycythaemia (EPO)**, **hypercalcaemia (PTHrP)**, hypertension (renin), **Stauffer syndrome** (non-metastatic hepatic dysfunction); left varicocele that does not empty lying down (left renal vein tumour thrombus).
Testicular tumour → **high inguinal orchidectomy** (never scrotal approach; para-aortic node drainage). LDH reflects tumour burden.

**Torsion**: bell-clapper deformity; salvage is high within **6 h** and falls steeply after; **Prehn sign** negative (pain not relieved by elevation); Doppler must not delay exploration; fix both testes.

**BPH**: arises in the **transition zone** (prostate cancer mainly peripheral zone); α-blockers (tamsulosin) for quick symptom relief, 5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride) shrink gland and lower PSA by ~50%; TURP for refractory/complicated.
**TURP syndrome**: absorption of hypotonic glycine irrigant → dilutional **hyponatraemia**, fluid overload, transient blindness (glycine); prevented by bipolar TURP with saline.

**Bladder cancer**: urothelial carcinoma (smoking, aniline dyes, cyclophosphamide); **SCC with schistosomiasis**; painless haematuria → cystoscopy + **TURBT**; high-risk NMIBC → intravesical **BCG**; muscle-invasive → neoadjuvant cisplatin chemo + radical cystectomy.

**PUV**: commonest cause of lower urinary tract obstruction in boys; **VCUG** shows dilated posterior urethra; antenatal USG — **keyhole sign**; treatment = endoscopic valve ablation (vesicostomy in small infants).

traps.stem: Testicular mass with markedly raised AFP; biopsy reported as seminoma. Interpretation?
traps.trap: Pure seminoma — treat as seminoma.
traps.fix: Pure seminoma does not raise AFP; an elevated AFP means a non-seminomatous (e.g. yolk sac) component — manage as NSGCT.

traps.stem: Suspected testicular tumour. Biopsy approach?
traps.trap: Trans-scrotal biopsy or scrotal orchidectomy.
traps.fix: High inguinal orchidectomy with early cord clamping; scrotal violation changes lymphatic drainage to inguinal nodes and risks seeding.

traps.stem: Child with abdominal mass crossing the midline with calcification on CT. Most likely?
traps.trap: Wilms tumour (most common renal tumour of childhood).
traps.fix: Crossing midline + calcification + age <2 suggests neuroblastoma; Wilms is intrarenal, rarely crosses midline and rarely calcifies.

cards.front: Investigation of choice for suspected ureteric colic?
cards.back: Non-contrast CT KUB (low-dose). USG first in pregnancy and children.

cards.text: Stone >{{c1::20 mm}} or staghorn → {{c2::PCNL}}; distal ureteric stone ≤10 mm → medical expulsive therapy with {{c3::tamsulosin}}.
Yolk sac tumour raises {{c1::AFP}} and shows {{c2::Schiller-Duval bodies}}; choriocarcinoma raises {{c3::β-hCG}}.

cards.front: Investigation of choice for posterior urethral valves?
cards.back: Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG/MCU): dilated, elongated posterior urethra with a thick bladder; treat by endoscopic valve ablation.

cards.text: Testicular torsion: explore within {{c1::6 hours}} for best salvage; {{c2::Prehn}} sign is negative and the {{c3::cremasteric}} reflex is absent.

title: Hernias & paediatric surgery (CDH, pyloric stenosis, Hirschsprung, TEF, NEC)
subject: Surgery
anchor: Groin lump above and medial to the pubic tubercle = inguinal; below and lateral = femoral (women, highest strangulation risk).
First-born boy, 3–6 weeks, non-bilious projectile vomiting, hungry after feeds, olive-shaped mass = hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
Newborn with frothing, choking on feeds, NG tube coiling in the pouch + gas in stomach = oesophageal atresia with distal TEF (Gross C).
algorithm:
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
  → USG (pyloric muscle thickness ≥3–4 mm, length ≥15–17 mm)
  → Correct dehydration and alkalosis FIRST (0.45–0.9% saline + dextrose + KCl once passing urine)
  → Ramstedt pyloromyotomy (open or laparoscopic) — not an emergency
Hirschsprung disease
  → Suspect: delayed meconium (>48 h), distension, explosive stool on PR (squirt sign)
  → Contrast enema: transition zone (do not prepare bowel); rectal suction biopsy = diagnostic
  → Decompress (rectal washouts) → pull-through (Swenson / Duhamel / Soave)
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
  → Avoid bag-mask ventilation; intubate + NG decompression → stabilise pulmonary hypertension → delayed repair

head: Hernia
Content / feature
rows: Only part of the antimesenteric bowel wall → strangulation without obstruction

points: **Hesselbach triangle**: medially lateral border of rectus abdominis, laterally inferior epigastric vessels, inferiorly inguinal ligament.

Inguinal canal walls (MALT): roof — internal oblique/transversus (conjoint), anterior — external oblique aponeurosis, floor — inguinal (lacunar) ligament, posterior — transversalis fascia + conjoint tendon.

**Femoral hernia**: neck below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, through the femoral canal (medial to femoral vein); **highest strangulation risk** → always repair; commoner in women, but inguinal hernia is still the commonest hernia in women.

**CDH**: **Bochdalek** (posterolateral, mostly left) is commonest; **Morgagni** (anterior, retrosternal, mostly right); mortality driven by **pulmonary hypoplasia + pulmonary hypertension**; scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in chest.
**Pyloric stenosis** metabolic picture: **hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis** with paradoxical aciduria; association with early **erythromycin** exposure.

**Hirschsprung**: absent ganglion cells in submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses of the distal bowel (rectosigmoid commonest); RET gene, Down syndrome; biopsy shows **↑ acetylcholinesterase-positive nerve fibres, absent calretinin**; risk of enterocolitis.

**Oesophageal atresia/TEF (Gross)**: **type C** (EA + distal TEF) commonest ~85%; type A pure EA = gasless abdomen; **H-type** (type E) presents later with recurrent pneumonia and coughing on feeds; look for **VACTERL**.

**NEC**: preterm, formula-fed, day 7–14; bilious aspirates, bloody stools; X-ray **pneumatosis intestinalis**, portal venous gas; modified **Bell staging**; pneumoperitoneum → laparotomy/peritoneal drain.
Infant inguinal hernia → herniotomy soon after diagnosis (high incarceration risk); umbilical hernia usually closes spontaneously by 4–5 years.

traps.stem: Baby with pyloric stenosis, pH 7.55, K⁺ 2.8, Cl⁻ 85. Take to theatre today?
traps.trap: Immediate pyloromyotomy because the diagnosis is confirmed.
traps.fix: Pyloric stenosis is a medical emergency, not a surgical one: correct dehydration, alkalosis and hypokalaemia first (risk of post-op apnoea with alkalosis), then pyloromyotomy.

traps.stem: Elderly woman with small bowel strangulation but no obstructive symptoms; tender groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
traps.trap: Simple irreducible inguinal hernia; no obstruction means no bowel compromise.
traps.fix: Femoral hernia with Richter type: only part of the bowel wall is trapped, so it can strangulate without obstruction. Emergency repair.

traps.stem: Newborn with respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds in the left chest. First step?
traps.trap: Bag-and-mask ventilation.
traps.fix: CDH: avoid bag-mask (distends herniated bowel, compresses lung); intubate, NG decompression, gentle ventilation; surgery after stabilisation.

cards.text: Boundaries of Hesselbach triangle: {{c1::inferior epigastric vessels}} laterally, {{c2::lateral border of rectus abdominis}} medially and {{c3::inguinal ligament}} inferiorly.

cards.front: Richter vs Littre vs Amyand hernia?
cards.back:
Richter: part of the bowel wall (antimesenteric) → strangulation without obstruction.
Littre: Meckel diverticulum.
Amyand: appendix in an inguinal hernia (de Garengeot: in a femoral hernia).

cards.text: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes {{c1::hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis}}; definitive surgery is {{c2::Ramstedt pyloromyotomy}}.

cards.front: Gold-standard diagnostic test for Hirschsprung disease and its findings?
cards.back: Rectal suction biopsy: absent ganglion cells, hypertrophied nerve trunks, ↑ acetylcholinesterase staining, absent calretinin.

cards.text: Commonest type of oesophageal atresia is {{c1::proximal atresia with distal TEF (Gross C)}}; {{c2::H-type}} fistula presents later with recurrent aspiration pneumonia.

subject: Surgery
anchor: ASA grades I–VI ('E' added for emergency); wound classes clean → clean-contaminated → contaminated → dirty predict SSI risk.
Fever and chills within the first hour of transfusion in a multiparous recipient? Think febrile non-haemolytic (commonest); hypoxia + bilateral infiltrates within 6 h, normal JVP = TRALI.
Prolene for vascular anastomosis; PDS/Vicryl absorbable; silk most reactive.

points: **ASA**: I healthy; II mild systemic disease; III severe systemic disease; IV severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life; V moribund, not expected to survive without the operation; VI brain-dead organ donor.

**Wound healing phases**: haemostasis → inflammation (neutrophils first, **macrophage is the key cell**) → proliferation (fibroblasts, type III collagen, angiogenesis, granulation) → remodelling (type III replaced by type I; scar reaches ~70–80% of normal strength, never 100%).
Vitamin C (hydroxylation of proline/lysine) and zinc are needed for collagen synthesis; steroids impair healing (vitamin A partly reverses it).

**Absorbable sutures**: catgut (natural; plain/chromic), polyglactin 910 (**Vicryl**), polyglycolic acid (Dexon), poliglecaprone (**Monocryl**), polydioxanone (**PDS** — longest-lasting). **Non-absorbable**: silk (natural, braided, most tissue reaction), nylon, polypropylene (**Prolene** — least thrombogenic, vascular anastomosis), polyester (Ethibond), stainless steel (sternal closure).
Synthetic absorbable sutures are absorbed by **hydrolysis** (less inflammation); catgut by **proteolysis**.
**Maintenance fluid (Holliday-Segar)**: 4 mL/kg/h for the first 10 kg, 2 mL/kg/h for the next 10 kg, 1 mL/kg/h thereafter; adult roughly 25–30 mL/kg/day water with ~1 mmol/kg/day Na⁺ and K⁺.

**Enteral feeding preferred** whenever the gut works (maintains mucosal barrier); start early post-op. **Refeeding syndrome**: hypophosphataemia (hallmark), hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency → start slowly, give thiamine.
Massive transfusion complications: **hypocalcaemia** (citrate), hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, dilutional coagulopathy.
**SSI prophylaxis**: single dose of cefazolin within 60 min before incision; redose for long surgery or major blood loss; not needed beyond 24 h.

traps.stem: Acute non-perforated appendicitis operated: wound class?
traps.trap: Dirty (class IV) because of inflamed appendix.
traps.fix: Acute non-purulent inflammation = contaminated (class III). Perforation/pus = dirty (class IV). Elective appendicectomy without inflammation = clean-contaminated.

traps.stem: Transfusion: dyspnoea, hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates within 2 h, JVP normal, BNP normal.
traps.trap: TACO — treat with diuretics.
traps.fix: TRALI (non-cardiogenic oedema, normal JVP/BNP, often hypotension). TACO has hypertension, raised JVP and BNP and responds to diuretics.

traps.stem: Best suture for a vascular anastomosis?
traps.trap: Silk — strong and traditional.
traps.fix: Polypropylene (Prolene): monofilament, non-absorbable, least thrombogenic and least reactive. Silk is the most reactive suture.

cards.text: ASA {{c1::IV}} = severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life; ASA {{c2::V}} = moribund patient not expected to survive without surgery.

cards.front: Wound class of a laparotomy for perforated appendix with pus?
cards.back: Class IV dirty-infected.

cards.text: The most important cell in wound healing is the {{c1::macrophage}}; immature granulation tissue contains type {{c2::III}} collagen, later replaced by type {{c3::I}}.

cards.front: Commonest transfusion reaction and its prevention?
cards.back: Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction; prevented by pre-storage leucoreduction.

cards.text: {{c1::Polypropylene (Prolene)}} is preferred for vascular anastomosis; {{c2::silk}} causes the most tissue reaction.
Hallmark electrolyte abnormality of refeeding syndrome is {{c1::hypophosphataemia}}.
